Point density reflects probability |ψ|². Denser regions = higher electron probability. Colour is discrete: blue or pink depending on the sign of ψ.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The bound electron

Let’s see what the electron is really doing. An electron held by a proton settles into standing waves ψnlm(r, θ, φ), labelled by three integers n, l and m. Every dot is one possible position, scattered with probability |ψ|² — blue where ψ is positive, pink where it’s negative. Surfaces carrying no dots at all are where ψ vanishes.

2 · The planetary picture

Let’s begin with an old favourite. In the Bohr model the electron circles the proton on an orbit of one fixed radius. For the ground state, where do you think repeated position measurements actually land?

3 · Counting the gaps

Now take a closer look at the gaps. At n = 2, l = 0 the cloud separates into an inner ball and an outer shell, divided by one spherical surface with no dots. What’s your guess — for a state (n, l), how many such spherical surfaces are there?

4 · At the proton itself

Let’s zoom right in on the centre. The s states put their densest dots right at the proton. Which orbitals do you think have any electron density there at all?

5 · Turning the orbital

One last change. The dumbbell on screen is the n = 2, l = 1, m = 0 state, aligned with z. Holding n and l fixed, m is changed to +1. What do you think happens to the energy?

About this simulation

The Physics

Hydrogen atom wavefunctions · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

An electron held by a proton has no orbit. It has a standing-wave state ψnlm, labelled by three integers. This sim draws any state up to n = 7 as a cloud of dots or a flat slice, so you can see what each integer changes.

What you'll learn

  • How the integers n, l and m label a state, and which values each can take.
  • How dot density relates to the wavefunction, and what the colours mean.
  • How the empty surfaces inside a cloud depend on n and l.
  • How the readout tiles depend on n, l and m.
A sketch: dots around the proton, blue where ψ > 0 and pink where ψ < 0.

What's on screen

  • Blue dots: places where ψ > 0.
  • Pink dots: places where ψ < 0.
  • Gaps: surfaces where ψ = 0 and no dots appear.
  • X, Y, Z axes (white).
  • Orbital properties (sidebar): the state's name and eight readout tiles.
See itShow the 2px orbital. Watch for: two clouds of dots on opposite sides of the proton, one blue and one pink.

03

Three integers label each state

The electron feels only the 1/r pull of the proton. The Schrödinger equation for that pull has stationary solutions, each picked out by three integers.

Kinetic energy plus the Coulomb pull: the whole atom is this line.
Each state splits into a radial factor (how far out) and an angular factor (which way).
  • n = 1, 2, 3, … labels the radial pattern. l = 0 to n − 1 labels the angular shape and is written s, p, d, f, g for 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. m = −l to +l labels the orientation about the z axis.
  • Dots. Dot density follows |ψ|², a probability per unit volume. The probability of a region is |ψ|² times its volume.
  • Colour. ψ is real here: blue marks ψ > 0, pink ψ < 0. Only |ψ|² decides where dots land.
  • Real orbitals. For m ≠ 0 the sim draws cos(|m|φ) for m > 0 and sin(|m|φ) for m < 0, so |2, 1, 1⟩ is px and |2, 1, −1⟩ is py.
See itShow the 3dxy orbital (m = −2) as a flat slice. Watch for: the xy plane in four quadrants, alternately blue and pink, meeting along the x and y axes.
04

The 1s cloud is densest at the proton

In the 1s state the dots crowd at the proton and thin smoothly outward. No ring or shell is singled out. R10 ∝ e−r/a₀, so |ψ|² at r = 1 a₀ is e−2 ≈ 0.14 of its value at the proton.

That does not make the proton the likeliest distance. The probability of finding the electron between r and r + dr is r²R² dr, because the shell at radius r has volume 4πr² dr. For 1s this peaks at r = a₀, the Bohr radius.

Rnl (top) and r²R² (bottom) for 1s and 2s. The 2s curve crosses zero at r = 2 a₀; section 05 explains why.
  • Density |ψ|² (what the dots show) is largest at r = 0.
  • Distance distribution r²R² (what a ruler would record) peaks at 1 a₀.
See itShow the 1s ground state. Watch for: the brightest, most crowded dots at the centre, thinning smoothly outward with no ring.
05

A state has n − 1 nodal surfaces, of two kinds

A node is a surface where ψ = 0, so no dots land there. ψ changes sign across it, so the colour flips from blue to pink. The two factors of ψnlm each supply nodes.

The radial factor is an exponential, a power of ρ, and a polynomial L of degree n − l − 1 (ρ = 2r/na₀).
  • Radial nodes are spheres where that polynomial is zero. There are n − l − 1 of them. 2s has one, at r = 2 a₀; 3p has one, at r = 6 a₀.
  • Angular nodes are the zeros of the angular factor: l surfaces through the proton, planes or cones.
  • Total = (n − l − 1) + l = n − 1. The sim's three node tiles show these counts.
See itShow the 3pz orbital. Watch for: pink above and blue below, a small blue-and-pink pair at the centre, and the node tiles reading 1, 1 and 2.
06

Only s states have density at the proton

Near the proton the radial factor behaves like ρl, the middle factor in section 05's formula. For l = 0 that is 1, so R and |ψ|² stay finite at r = 0 and dots reach the proton. For l ≥ 1, ρl is zero at r = 0, so |ψ|² = 0 there and ∝ r2l close by.

  • Size. At r = 0.1 a₀, R is 0.64 for 2s and 0.019 for 2p (units of a₀−3/2).
  • Why. Angular momentum adds a term ħ²l(l + 1)/2μr² to the radial equation. It repels the wave from r = 0, more strongly for larger l.
  • Picture. A p orbital's two lobes meet only at a point, with a nodal plane through the proton.
See itCompare 2s with 2pz in slice mode. Watch for: 2s bright at the proton, then 2pz bright above and below it, about 2 a₀ away, with a dark line between them.
07

Energy depends on n alone

The laws behind the tiles. g = 2n² is n² orbitals times 2 spin states; the sim draws only the spatial part.
  • Energy. En = −13.6 eV / n². Negative means bound. The tile reads −13.600 eV at n = 1 and −3.400 eV at n = 2, and it ignores l and m. All 2s and 2p states sit on one level. This is a feature of a pure 1/r pull.
  • |L| = √(l(l + 1)) ħ, never lħ: 1.414 ħ for l = 1.
  • Lz. For m = 0 the tile reads 0 ħ. For m ≠ 0 the shape is an equal mix of +|m| and −|m|. Lz would come out +|m|ħ or −|m|ħ with equal chances, so the tile shows ⟨Lz⟩ = 0.
  • ⟨r⟩ = (a₀/2)[3n² − l(l + 1)] grows roughly as n². That is why the sim's view box reaches ±(2.5n² + 4) a₀.
n l m

These sliders drive the sim's n, l and m dropdowns, with the same nesting.

See itStep through 2s, 2pz and 2px. Watch for: the energy tile staying at −3.400 eV while |L| and Lz change.
08

Where it matters

  • Spectral lines. A jump between levels emits a photon with λ = hc/ΔE. n = 3 → 2 gives 1.89 eV, 656 nm, hydrogen's red line. n = 2 → 1 gives 10.2 eV, 122 nm, in the ultraviolet. The sim shows states, not jumps.
  • Chemistry. The s, p and d shapes are the vocabulary of atomic orbitals. In atoms with more electrons the shapes stay similar, but the levels split by l.
  • Rydberg atoms. For l = 0, ⟨r⟩ = 1.5n² a₀, so n = 100 gives 15 000 a₀, about 0.8 µm. The sim stops at n = 7.
Go deeper: photon wavelengths, and why l does not matter
h c = 1239.84 eV·nm. The sim prints levels, never photons.
  • E depending on n alone is special to the 1/r force, which has an extra conserved quantity, the Runge–Lenz vector.
  • Real hydrogen splits these levels slightly (relativity, spin, the Lamb shift): about 5 × 10−5 eV at n = 2. The sim shows the leading result.
See itShow the 7s state. Watch for: the ⟨r⟩ tile reading 73.5 a₀, 49 times the 1s value, and a cloud of many shells.
09

Summary

In one line. Three integers label a hydrogen state; the dots show |ψ|², which has n − 1 nodal surfaces, and the energy depends on n alone.

Key points

  • ψnlm = Rnl(r) · Ylm(θ, φ), with l = 0 to n − 1 and m = −l to +l.
  • Dot density is |ψ|² per unit volume; colour is the sign of ψ.
  • n − l − 1 spherical nodes plus l planes or cones. Only l = 0 reaches the proton.
  • En = −13.6 eV / n², |L| = √(l(l + 1)) ħ, and ⟨r⟩ = (a₀/2)[3n² − l(l + 1)].

Common mix-ups

  • "The electron circles the proton at the Bohr radius." a₀ is the likeliest distance for 1s, not an orbit.
  • "Blue and pink are positive and negative charge." They are the sign of ψ. Only |ψ|² says where the electron is likely.
  • "2px carries Lz = +ħ." It is an equal mix of m = +1 and −1: Lz is +ħ or −ħ with equal chances, averaging 0.

Things to try on your own

  • Pick a state with n = 4. Work out its node counts from n and l, then check the tiles.
  • Load 5g and compute ⟨r⟩ by hand. Compare with the tile.
  • Compare 3dz² with 3dxy: count lobes and colour changes, then compare their energy tiles.
